title: The Coolest New Wired Headphones to Keep on Your Hi-Fi Wishlist (Updated)
summary: We've rounded up the latest wired headphone releases from Grado Labs, Audio-Technica, Sony, Audeze, Meze Audio and more.
content: We’ve rounded up the latest wired headphone releases from Grado Labs, Audio-Technica, Sony, Audeze, Meze Audio and more. All are new for 2026. Gear Patrol If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more Even in this age of wireless audio, traditional wired hi-fi isn’t going anywhere. Wired headphones are still more reliable and just easier to “plug and play.” There’s no need to worry about running out of battery. And despite advances in Bluetooth codecs, a physical wired connection can still deliver much higher-resolution audio. Plus, traditional audio brands continue to release new pairs of wired headphones and in-ear monitors, catered to both rising hi-fi enthusiasts and seasoned audiophiles. Below, we’ve rounded up the most notable wired hi-fi releases so far this year. All models have been announced (or released) in 2026. The Best New Wired Headphones of 2026 (January – November) Noble Audio Noble Audio Paladin Noble Audio’s Paladin is a high-end pair of in-ear monitors (IEMs) that are wrapped in shining armor, literally. They get their name from a paladin, a medieval knight, and have a distinctive appearance meant to look like chainmail. It consists of a woven pattern of small, interlocking rings with silver-finished resin shells. Inside, the Paladin IEMs are certified audiophile-grade. Each earbud has a 12-driver tribrid configuration comprising eight balanced armatures, two Sonion bone-conduction drivers and two Super-Magnetic planar drivers. A multi-way passive crossover brings the three driver technologies together. read more $3,500 at Bloom Audio Klipsch Klipsch Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 The Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 are Klipsch’s first pair of over-ear wired headphones in over a decade. Both are similar designed, with real wood earcups and feature copper-ring accents, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, and a protein-leather headband. The difference between the two is that the HP-2 is a closed-back headphone, while the HP-3 is a semi-open-back headphone. Both headphones are highly efficient and easy to drive, so they can work in a wide range of listening setups. Both aim to deliver full-range sound with very little distortion. read more $1,000 at Klipsch (HP-2) $1,200 at Klipsch (HP-3) Audio-Technica Audio-Technica ATH-AWX7000 The Audio-Technica ATH-AWX7000 is the brand’s new flagship pair of closed-back wired headphones. Their most striking feature is gorgeous wooden housings made from Kiso cypress, one of Japan’s finest woods, and hand-finished with Echizen lacquer. But A-T has made sure that they sound as good as they look. Each pair has the brand’s new True Closed-back Acoustic (TCbA) design, which harnesses air pressure generated within the enclosed earcups. They also have new driver technologies that enable the ATH-AWX7000 to reveal “subtle details even within complex and familiar recordings.” read more $3,799 at Audio-Technica Sony Sony MDR-3R The Sony MDR-3R is a modern take on the brand’s original MDR-3 headphones that were released in 1979 and debuted alongside the Walkman TPS-L2 player. The MDR-3R retains the original lightweight, open-ear design and features swappable blue and orange ear pads, letting users switch based on their mood or preferences. The biggest change is they have of a USB-C jack to connect directly to today’s smartphones and laptops. The cable also features a line-in microphone and remote for calls and adjusting volume and playback. read more $60 at Sony $80 at Sony (Stranger Things Edition) Campfire Audio Campfire Audio Cascara Mk2 The Cascara Mk2 is the second-generation version of Campfire Audio’s original Cascara IEMs. They feature the 10mm dual-magnet dynamic driver, which the brand describes as being valued for its rich, warm transients, deep-reaching bass, real texture, and smooth, detailed highs. But they have an updated look and subtle tuning refinements to help deliver smoother high frequencies. read more $549 at Campfire Audio Grado Grado Signature S150 Grado’s Signature S150 is the most affordable pair of open-back wired headphones in the brand’s high-end Signature series. It retains Grado’s “signature” retro aesthetic that combines metal components with a gorgeous leather headband and plush ear cushions. It features a new 44mm S driver with a paper-composite diaphragm that Grado says is based on technology used in the larger 52mm S drivers in its HP100 SE ($2,495) and S950 ($2,195) headphones. According to the brand, the S150 “delivers a level of clarity and detail that challenges expectations for a headphone in its class, while preserving the natural body and musical character of the performance.” read more $295 at Grado Audio-Technica Audio-Technica ATH-AWX7000 The Audio-Technica ATH-AWX7000 is the brand’s new flagship pair of closed-back wired headphones. Their most striking feature is gorgeous wooden housings made from Kiso cypress, one of Japan’s finest woods, and hand-finished with Echizen lacquer. But A-T has made sure that they sound as good as they look. Each pair has the brand’s new True Closed-back Acoustic (TCbA) design, which harnesses air pressure generated within the enclosed earcups. They also have new driver technologies that enable the ATH-AWX7000 to reveal “subtle details even within complex and familiar recordings.” read more $3,799 at Audio-Technica Grado Grado Signature S550 The Signature S550 is the most affordable pair of open-back headphones in Grado’s flagship Signature series. Positioned as more affordable alternatives to the brand’s Signature S750, which are nearly twice as expensive, the S550 has the same 50mm S2 dynamic drivers, but they have been tuned specifically for its all-wood enclosure (instead of wood, the Signature S750 has an all-aluminum housing). According to the brand, they offer “a more relaxed presentation while preserving the speed, detail, and immediacy that have long defined the Grado sound.” read more $995 at Grado Fiio Fiio FT15 The Fiio FT15 is a midrange open-back headphone with planar magnetic drivers. They are new-and-improved versions of the brand’s FT5, which were released in late 2023. The main upgrade in the FT15 is a thinner diaphragm (the membrane inside the driver) and a larger driver, which together promise a more natural sound and a wider soundstage. Additionally, Fiio gave the FT15 earcups that are made of real wood, so no two pairs look exactly alike. read more $500 at Apos Bose Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds The Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds is the company’s first new pair of wired earbuds in over a decade. The main difference compared to other in-ear headphones is that, as their name gives away, they support active noise-cancellation. The earbuds have an inline remote for playback controls and switching between modes: ANC on/off and transparency. They also support lossless audio up to 24-bit/48kHz. The earbuds have a USB-C connection, making them “plug-and-play ready” with today’s smartphones. read more $99 at Bose $99 at Best Buy Meze Audio Meze Audio Alba S Meze’s Alba has been the Romanian hi-fi brand’s most affordable pair of wired in-ear monitors since its release in 2024. One of the things that has made the Alba unique is that Meze ships it with a custom 3.5mm-to-USB-C adapter with its own built-in DAC. However, if you already own an external DAC/adapter (or you just don’t want one), Meze now offers the Alba S . It’s the same wired headphone, but doesn’t ship with adapter and costs $30 less. read more $129 at Meze Audio (% off) Audeze Audeze LCD-5s Audeze has introduced next-generation versions of its flagship planar magnetic headphones, the LCD-5, which were released in 2021. As the “s” in their name suggests, the most notable aspect of the LCD-5s is that they have been integrated with the brand’s Symmetric Linear Acoustic Modulator (SLAM) technology, which promises to help them deliver deeper bass and a wider soundstage than their predecessors. The American headphone maker claims that the LCD-5s “represents the pinnacle of planar magnetic engineering and luxury build.” read more $4,500 at Audeze Meze Audio Meze Strada Meze’s Strada is a new pair of closed-back headphones with dynamic drivers that are designed to look as good as they sound. Each pair is made of high-end materials, combining a magnesium frame (hand-painted deep green) with Macassar ebony hardwood ear cups — ensuring that no two are alike — and the ear cushions and a headband are both made out of genuine leather. They feature the same 50mm dynamic drivers as the brand’s 109 Pro open-back headphones, which cost $799, but they’ve been tuned for closed-back performance. Meze claims that they “set a new benchmark in closed-back dynamic headphones.” read more $799 at Meze Audio Sony Sony IER-M500 The Sony IER-M500 is brand’s new entry-level pair of wired in-ear monitors. According to the brand, they’re “the perfect partner for amateur, emerging, and professional musicians, performers, and monitor engineers who require reliable and accurate in-ear monitoring for live performances and practices.” Sony is offering them in three transparent color options. Black and clear are the most straightforward options, while the red/blue option has the two earbuds in different colors. read more $120 at Sony $120 at Amazon Fiio Fiio Snowsky Nature The Snowsky Nature is a pair of over-ear, closed-back wired headphones that cost just $39. They get their name from a “nature-inspired industrial design” meant to look like real wood but made mostly of plastic (which helps keep them lightweight and affordable). They feature newly engineered 50mm dynamic drivers, which the brand says were “developed to reproduce music with greater authority, lower distortion, and improved realism.” read more $39 at AliExpress Final Audio Final DX10000 CL The Final DX10000 CL is the company’s new flagship pair of closed-back wired headphones. They’re built around a newly developed 40mm True Diamond diaphragm dynamic driver, designed to combat the resonance and coloration that typically hinder closed-back headphones. According to the brand, the headphones are “designed for listeners who want a private, immersive and physically engaging listening experience, with the clarity, tonal accuracy and resolution expected from a true flagship audiophile product.” read more $8,499 at Final Audio Audio-Technica Audio-Technica ATH‑WP900SE The Audio-Technica ATH-WP900SE (or special edition ATH-WP900) is a pair of closed-back wired headphones that is a joint collaboration with Fujigen, the iconic Japanese guitar brand, as their earcups are made of the same maple hardwood that it exclusively uses to build its guitars. These special edition models feature Fujigen’s iconic 3‑tone sunburst lacquer finish and, according to the brand, pay homage to the “timeless beauty of classic instruments.” It marks the first time Audio-Technica has applied the popular lacquer finish to any of its headphones. read more $969 at Audio-Technica Meze Audio Meze Arta The Romanian hi-fi company specializes in high-end planar magnetic headphones. And now with the Arta, it has a new flagship. They have a sculptural design, are made of premium materials (including carbon fiber and leather) and feature a Rinaro High Impedance Isodynamic Hybrid Array MZ5 HΩ driver, which Meze Audio claims is the highest-impedance planar magnetic headphone driver to date. According to the brand, the Arta headphones “deliver a rich, speaker-like presentation with lifelike detail, offering the most immersive sonic experience we have ever created.” read more $6,000 at Meze Audio Audeze Audeze MM-520 The California-based hi-fi specialist has introduced the MM-520, a pair of open-back, over-ear headphones designed for musicians and audio professionals. They’re an updated version of the company’s MM-500 studio headphones, as they have the same general design and feature the same 90mm planar magnetic drivers. The main upgrade with the MM-520 is the integration of Audeze’s SLAM (Symmetric Linear Acoustic Modulator) technology, which the brand says should improve the headphone’s bass accuracy and spatial detail. read more $1,699 at Audeze Astell&Kern Astell&Kern Clarus The Astell&Kern Clarus is the brand’s latest high-end pair of in-ear monitors. They are designed around a 9-driver tribrid architecture, featuring a dynamic driver for low frequencies, balanced armature drivers for mids and highs, and MEMS drivers for ultra-high frequencies. Each earbud is constructed of 6061-T6 aluminum. According to Astell&Kern, the Clarus is designed to deliver transparent and distortion-free audio exactly as the artist intended. At the time of writing, price and availability info have not yet been released. read more Learn More Campfire Audio Campfire Audio Chimera The Chimera is the Portland-based audio maker’s most high-end and expensive pair of in-ear monitors. Each earbud features a unique nine-driver architecture that combines four distinct driver technologies: dynamic, balanced armature, electrostatic and bone conduction. (In fact, it’s the first time Campfire Audio has incorporated a conduction driver and embedded it directly into its CNC-machined magnesium shell.) The result, according to the brand, “is a listening experience that is both highly detailed and physically engaging.” The Chimera ships with an ALO Audio Valence-6 cable featuring four high-purity copper conductors and two 50/50 copper-silver-plated conductors. read more $7,500 at Campfire Audio Activo Activo Scoop The Activo Scoop is an affordable pair of IEMs that come with detachable cables and adapters for USB-C, 3.5mm and 4.4mm (balanced), so you can use them with your smartphone, laptop, portable games console and dedicated hi-fi player. According to the brand, they promise a combination of flexibility and performance rarely seen at this price point. read more $99 at Activo Final Audio Final DX4000CL The Final DX4000CL is the newest addition to the brand’s DX series of closed-back wired headphones, slotting between its $599 DX3000CL and its flagship $1,999 DX6000CL. And like those other headphones, the DX4000CL aims to deliver a more natural, balanced sound than traditional closed-back headphones, which often lean toward bass-heavy sound. read more $999 at Final Meze Audio Meze Astru The Astru is the Romanian hi-fi brand’s most premium pair of in-ear monitors to date. According to the brand, they are meant for “listeners who demand true high-end performance without crossing into flagship pricing territory.” The earbuds feature a 10mm multilayer composite dynamic driver diaphragm, meticulously engineered to balance speed, control, and musical weight. They have a beautiful titanium housing, detachable cables and feature a gold-plated 4.4 mm balanced termination. A 3.5mm adapter is included so you can use it with most traditional sources. read more $899 at Meze Audio Sennheiser Sennheiser HD 400U The Sennheiser HD 400U is a pair of closed-back wired headphones with dynamic drivers. They are a new version of the company’s HD 400S, which was released in early 2019. The big update with the 400U is that they feature a USB-C wired connection (instead of traditional 3.5mm jack) and thus are better suited for modern smartphones and laptops. They support lossless audio up to 24-bit/96kHz. Best of all? The cost just $100. read more $100 at Sennheiser Moondrop Moondrop Skyland Moondrop’s Skyland is a wired, open-back headphone with planar magnetic drivers. Each pair features large 100mm planar magnetic drivers with an ultra-thin 500nm diaphragm, which is designed to move quickly and accurately, and ultimately deliver an incredibly detailed sound. They also incorporate Full Drive Technology (FDT), which the brand claims helps them achieve performance levels closer to those of electrostatic headphones. read more $800 at Bloom Audio

title: Nothing Is Running a Killer Black Friday Sale on Its Flagship Earbuds and Headphones
summary: The game-changing tech brand has sales as much as 43 percent off this week.
content: The game-changing tech brand has sales as much as 43 percent off this week. Nothing If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more For a company called Nothing , there’s a whole lot going on. Welcome to Shop Smarter : A series dedicated to highlighting not just what’s on sale, but why it’s worth owning. Discover more here . Founded in London in 2020, Carl Pei’s tech brand has aimed to create products that bring a sense of intrigue to the consumer. Instead of replicating the same general design as other smartphones and earbuds, Nothing injects its own unique design language. Its signature see-through hardware, playful use of color and distinctive LED lighting turned otherwise familiar products into seriously cool conversation pieces. What originally began as a way to pare back the Android phone design has now expanded into headphones, earbuds and an increasingly broad ecosystem of connected devices. In other words, Nothing isn’t just trying to make different-looking tech. It’s trying to make technology fun again. Right now, the brand is running a rather impressive Black Friday sale , which is highlighted by its headphones and earbuds, but there are some smartphones thrown in the mix as well. Even its budget-friendly CMF sub-brand features some notable sales. Below are a few of our favorites. Nothing Nothing Headphones 1 The Headphones 1 are Nothing’s first-ever pair of wireless over-ear headphones. They have a similar striking design with transparent elements as the brand’s smartphones and wireless earbuds. And, most interestingly, Nothing partnered with KEF, the British hi-fi maker, to ensure that the headphones sound great. Additionally, the Headphones have active noise-cancellation and transparency modes. And they promise up to 35 hours of battery with ANC turned on. read more $169 at Nothing $299 (43% off) Nothing Nothing Headphone (1) Pro Nothing’s Headphone (1) Pro is the brand’s most high-end and expensive pair of wireless noise-canceling headphones to date. At $399, they’re designed to compete with the flagship models from Apple, Sony, Bose and other hi-fi brands. The Headphone (1) Pro retains the striking design of the predecessors (including semi-transparent earcups), but adds a triple-driver system for superior sound and a 10-mic system for more advanced noise-cancellation. The headphones include several “pro” features, including support for LDAC and 24-bit high-res audio. Most interestingly, they have a “Flat” switch that turns off the built-in equalizer and spatial audio and, according to the brand, “provides a neutral sound profile for producers and creators.” read more $319 at Nothing $399 (20% off) Nothing Nothing Ear (3a) When it comes to $100 earbuds, it’s difficult to beat Nothing’s Ear A series. The 3rd-gen model, the 3a, has just been updated with 32MB of built-in storage for recording calls, activated with the pinch of your fingers. After that, the recordings are sent automatically to your Nothing X app. The drivers have been upgraded as well to 12mm, giving you fuller hi-res quality. Along with the usual black, white and yellow colorways, a new pink is also thrown into the mix. read more $69 at Nothing $99 (30% off) Nothing Nothing Ear (open) Nothing’s Ear (open) ditches the in-ear seal in favor of open-ear sound, letting ambient noise in by design rather than by accident. A lightweight silicone hook keeps them locked in place during runs, lifts and anything else that gets your heart rate up, while IP54 water resistance handles sweat and light rain with no issue. With 30 hours of total battery life and Nothing’s signature transparent aesthetic, they’re built for people who want their music and their surroundings at the same time. read more $84 at Nothing $99 (15% off) Nothing CMF by Nothing Headphone Pro The CMF Headphone Pro packs up to 100 hours of battery life and active noise cancellation that blocks up to 99 percent of ambient noise into an over-ear frame aimed squarely at budget-conscious listeners. Interchangeable ear cushions let you swap the look and feel on the fly, giving the headphones a degree of personalization that’s rare at this price point. Available in three colorways read more $49 at Nothing $79 (38% off) Nothing Nothing CMF Clip Pro Nothing’s budget-friendly brand, CMF, has its first pair of open-ear wireless earbuds. The CMF Clip Pro are earbuds with a clip-on design, popularized by Bose’s Open Ultra Earbuds, that grip the outside of your ears sort of like earrings. They are designed to play music while also letting ambient sounds in, so they’re safer to wear when running, biking or exercising in public. One of their standout features is the charging case’s smart dial, which lets you adjust volume and control playback without touching the earbuds or your smartphone. Available in three colors: Dark Grey, Light Grey and Coral. read more $69 at Nothing $99 (30% off) Nothing CMF Speaker M The CMF Speaker M packs a two-driver system (a 70mm woofer and 16mm tweeter) into a milk-carton-inspired frame that handles 35W of output across a 60Hz – 20,000Hz range. IP68 protection, up to 18 hours of battery life and Bluetooth 6.0 with a 100-meter range make it a capable outdoor companion, while NFC Fast Pair, USB-C lossless audio and Auracast Party Mode offer flexibility for home use. You can also customize these with removable panels and freely available 3D-print files. read more $79 at Nothing $109 (28% off) Nothing Nothing Phone 3 Nothing’s Phone 3 is the company’s first true flagship smartphone. It maintains the standout transparent design of its predecessors, but it’s built with more premium materials, features an upgraded processor (Snapdragon 8S Gen 4), and has a flagship-worthy triple-camera system on its back. One significant change from Nothing’s other smartphones is that, instead of a Glyph interface (an array of customizable light strips on its back), the Phone 3 features a small circular LED display in the top-right corner of its back, which it calls the Glyph Matrix. This can show little images or emojis to give you an idea of what kind of notification you’ve received without having to flip the phone over. read more Starts at $499 $699 (29% off) About the Author: Ethan Brehm is an associate editor at Gear Patrol writing about footwear, watches, spirits, EDC and more. title: These Affordable Amplifiers Are Some of the Hottest Components in Modern Hi-Fi
summary: Just add speakers.
content: Just add speakers. Wiim If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more WiiM has become quite the disruptor in the budget hi-fi space over recent years. The California-based audio company is now well known for its streaming amplifiers (and wireless streamers), which are just as easy to use but significantly less expensive than rival options from Sonos and Bluesound. These streaming amplifiers are “just add speakers”hi-fi components. You plug them into power, connect them with a pair of passive bookshelf speakers and — boom! — you’ve got a modern stereo setup that supports Bluetooth and Wi-Fi streaming. The Vibelink Amp (bottom) stacked with the WiiM Ultra (top), the brand’s high-end streamer. WiiM Today, WiiM makes several streaming amplifiers. The WiiM Amp and WiiM Amp Pro are its two most entry-level options, with the latter promising slightly improved audio quality. The WiiM Amp Ultra adds more power and a beautiful display for showing album artwork. The WiiM Amp Pro is paired with a turntable and a set of bookshelf speakers. WiiM The WiiM Amp Ultra adds more power and a color screen for showing album artwork (along with various menus and settings). Wiim Additionally, WiiM also released its first non-streaming amplifier, the Vibelink Amp , in case you want a more traditional hi-fi setup. WiiM’s catalog of amplifiers is perfect for anybody looking to breathe new life into an unused pair of bookshelf speakers. And for Black Friday/Cyber Monday, all of them are on sale. You can check out the deals below. title: The Defender’s Spiritual Successor Is Making a Move Land Rover Never Did
summary: The Grenadier is making a break for the New World in an effort to capitalize on stateside promise.
content: The Grenadier is making a break for the New World in an effort to capitalize on stateside promise. Ineos If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more From safari rigs and overlanding conversions to public service and military vehicles , Ineos has been eager to have its Grenadier pick up where the Defender left off. Welcome to Power Moves : Diving deep into the product and brand moves that can change where a category is headed. Discover more here . Of course, as the Land Rover icon’s spiritual successor, the 4×4 is purpose-built to take up such responsibilities. Be it the simple utilitarian design or the standard off-road equipment, it stays close to what made the Defender … the Defender. Clearly, Ineos isn’t afraid to embrace the Stars and Stripes. Ineos However, Ineos is now preparing to make a move that Land Rover never did with the SUV while it was in production. I think it could have big implications for the brand. Grenadier green card I’m talking about Ineos’s decision to begin production of the Grenadier and the Quartermaster in the United States. As part of a recent announcement, the brand confirmed that it has shortlisted sites, aiming to finalize a decision in the coming months and have the facility operational in 2028. A relocation from the Hambach plant frees the facility for sale to BYD. Ineos As with Audi, Hyundai and other automakers, the move is financially motivated. Establishing a stateside presence circumvents the USA’s 25 percent tariff imposed on EU exports and the 25 percent chicken tax applicable to light-duty trucks. According to Ineos, it’s a market worth investing in. The USA has supposedly accounted for 70 percent of the Grenadier’s global sales, a respectable feat when considering the vehicle’s various fleet applications. Ineos’s move to the USA gives its Quartermaster a leg up on any rumored Defender trucks from the Stellantis/JLR MOU. Ineos It’s slated to be a full relocation, too. Though the brand intends to keep production going at the Hambach, France, plant in the medium term, it is currently in exclusive sale negotiations with BYD. Declaration of independence Beyond the practical import advantages that come with a stateside production shift, I think Ineos’s move could benefit the Grenadier’s image, too. Ineos currently leverages the Britishness of its vehicle, despite building it at a French plant. Ineos That’s chiefly because it could finally give the brand the space it needs to stand apart as something more than a Defender successor. After all, in addition to the parallels in purpose and design, Ineos leans into the Britishness of the vehicle with the “born in a pub” backstory. It only helps its Land Rover-like appeal. Still, that’s already a little murky because of the current production site in France. Accordingly, a move to the USA would allow Ineos to, if not reinvent, at least pivot in how it chooses to present the Grenadier. Ineos’s move stands to improve name recognition through an anchored manufacturing presence. Ineos And that’s not even addressing the effect that this kind of development will have on brand recognition. With some local presence and a little Made in USA sympathy to anchor the Ineos name, I’d imagine it’ll become far less niche. In any case, it’s a fortuitous development during America’s 250th year. If all goes well, like the colonies before it, Ineos is making a move across the pond that may be just the beginning of something bigger. Availability and pricing If you’re already ready to scoop up an Ineos Grenadier, it’s available in Station Wagon and Quartermaster forms starting at $71,750 and $86,300. title: Shower Thoughts: Why Does Every Passenger-Side Mirror Have That ‘Closer Than They Appear’ Warning?
summary: It's one of the most-read phrases in automotive history, and most drivers have no idea why it's there — or why the driver's side mirror skips it entirely.
content: Gear Patrol Studios It’s one of the most-read phrases in automotive history, and most drivers have no idea why it’s there — or why the driver’s side mirror skips it entirely. Welcome to Shower Thoughts of a Gear Head, where we chase down the surprisingly complicated answers to questions that show up uninvited at 7 a.m , in partnership with Klarna . Because when you’re not worried about money you’re free to think about anything else. You’ve stared at it a hundred times from the passenger seat: that eight-word warning stamped across the bottom of your side mirror. And every single time you have thought, Huh, I should look that up . Then you forgot. We did too, until now. Turns out it is a federal law, and the physics behind it are more interesting than you’d expect. A brief history of automobile rear-view mirrors Side mirrors started life as aftermarket accessories in the 1920s. By the mid-1960s, automakers offered a factory-optional right-side mirror — including on the 1964 – 1966 Ford Mustang. In 1967, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration issued Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 111 (FMVSS 111), which initially permitted only flat, non-magnifying mirrors on passenger cars. The convex passenger-side mirror existed, but the federal rulebook hadn’t yet made room for it. The optics: what a convex mirror actually does to your perception of distance A convex mirror bows outward, bending incoming light across a wider angle so a single piece of glass captures far more of the scene behind the car than a flat mirror of the same size. The tradeoff is compression: spreading a wide field of view across a small surface makes every object in the reflection appear smaller — and your brain reads smaller as farther away. Driver’s side vs. passenger’s side: why the asymmetry is intentional, not accidental The driver’s-side mirror is flat. Because the driver sits close to it, a flat mirror delivers an accurate, undistorted reflection with a wide enough field of view to be useful. The passenger-side mirror sits much farther from the driver’s eye line, so a flat mirror of the same size would show a dangerously narrow slice of the lane. The convex curve solves that coverage problem but introduces the distance distortion — which is exactly why the warning exists. The federal rule: how the government decided exactly how big the letters had to be Federal rules first required the warning on convex mirrors beginning in September 1971, covering the 1972 model year. Then on September 2, 1982, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) amended FMVSS 111 to formally allow convex glass on the passenger side of passenger cars. Convex mirrors became standard throughout the 1980s, and the warning label came with every one of them. Under 49 CFR § 571.111, Section S5.4.2, the exact phrase “Objects in Mirror Are Closer Than They Appear” must be permanently etched along the lower edge of every convex mirror, in letters between 4.8mm and 6.4mm tall. The wording, placement and size range are all mandatory. From Jurassic Park to Meat Loaf, the most famous eight words on any car Few pieces of regulatory copy have broken into popular culture the way this warning has. The mirror reflection in Jurassic Park — T. rex bearing down, those seven words visible in the glass — became one of the most recognized movie images of the 1990s. Jim Steinman wrote a variation of the phrase into a Meat Loaf song title. It has appeared on T-shirts, tattoos and internet memes ever since. Not bad for a line written by federal regulators to pass a safety standard.

title: Here’s What Happens When Toyota’s Workhorse Pickup Isn’t Built for Truck Stuff
summary: The automaker has revealed a sweet take on the Hilux that bucks everything you'd expect from the nameplate.
content: The automaker has revealed a sweet take on the Hilux that bucks everything you’d expect from the nameplate. Toyota If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more Toyota’s Hilux trucks have spent decades hauling cargo, surviving war zones and outlasting everything the world’s roughest terrain could throw at it. Top Gear famously put an example through hell and back to prove the nameplate’s mettle. Even then, the truck put up quite the fight. Toyota’s Hilux Travo Hyper Z Concept looks nothing like the stock truck. Toyota However, Toyota Thailand’s latest take on the truck does none of that. Instead, it strips away the Hilux’s utilitarian identity and reimagines it anew as a low-slung, wide-body aero machine. A transformed Travo Toyota is calling it the Hyper Z Concept, and it’s a build based on Thailand’s Travo Z Edition, a low-riding RWD alternative to the more traditional Hilux trims. The rear end easily makes for the most dramatic part of the transformation. Toyota To lean into that spirit even further, Toyota Thailand tapped Toyota Design Australia to design the wild body kit before you. It’s the product of two years’ development, and it shows. Around the front, the truck adopts a sweeping chin spoiler. Toyota ditched the auxiliary lights and replaced the front grille with bold Hilux-branded mesh. That dramatic first impression carries through in the side profile and in the lowered stance. The Hilux’s treatment also brings some widened wheel arches, cool branded dish covers and geometric side skirts. The rear diffuser and massive wing give the humble Hilux a brash Le Mans-esque style. Toyota Ultimately, however, it’s the rear end that’s the most transformative in its result. In place of the bed, Toyota has fitted a mammoth rear wing and some wild, sculpted aero bodywork that does away with any semblance of utility in favor of a Le Mans-like look. It all comes together in the detail choices. A sweet, glowing Hilux taillight in the center of the truck ties in the bold Hyper Z graphics, black roof and Toyota text on the wing. Focused interior upgrades put performance first. Toyota Street truck spirit In keeping with its untamed street truck aesthetics, Toyota’s Hilux Travo Hyper Z Concept brings some choice performance upgrades, too. For instance, to achieve its stance and camber, the truck rides on a custom suspension setup. In addition to some Öhlins remote-reservoir coilovers, the photos also show Swift springs, among other upgrades. Toyota hasn’t revealed drivetrain upgrades, but this pickup is begging for more power. Toyota The concept’s interior proves similarly driver-focused. Though it retains a four-door configuration, the Hilux’s cabin gains performance-grade additions like a three-spoke racing wheel, some bucket seats and a roll cage. Together with the upgraded dash unit in place of the stock instrument panel, the objective is readily clear. While Toyota hasn’t detailed any upgrades to the turbodiesel powertrain typically found in this version of the Hilux, it puts racing before pickup utility. Inspirational effort I don’t see the Travo Hyper Z moving beyond concept status. Instead, it stands as a design exercise from Toyota’s Thai division to prove that the Hilux Travo platform has real enthusiast potential despite its utilitarian focus. Even so, it’s a sweet effort; hopefully, it inspires similar treatments on other Toyota trucks, be it a KEI-01 or a Tacoma. Arc’teryx The SV stands for severe weather, and the brand built this shell for climbers who spend all day exposed to the elements atop high, alpine routes. In those conditions, a failed zipper or busted seam is not so much an inconvenience, but an actual problem. Undoubtedly, that level of protection isn’t cheap. Normally retailing at $900, it’s a steep investment for most, and it’s also one of the brand’s pieces that rarely gets a markdown. During its Black Friday sale, you can grab it for nearly $200 off. Built for severe mountainside protection This one is made durable. The shell is made from 100-denier Gore-Tex Pro ePE, the toughest and latest of Gore’s membranes. Arc’teryx actually helped develop the material to keep up with the brand’s high standards. Gore-Tex’s newly built 100-denier Gore-Tex Pro ePE is the thinnest, lightest yet equally as durable membrane to date. Arc’teryx It’s even thinner and lighter than Gore-Tex Pro while remaining equally durable. The burly nylon face can easily handle abrasion from rocks, ice, branches and pack straps. Plus, it keeps wind and water completely out. No stone is left unturned in its design, and even small details like WaterTight zippers are utilized, including pit zips to dump heat when the sun gets a little too warm. Add on RECCO reflectors in case of emergencies, a helmet-compatible hood and the fact that it weighs just over a pound, and you have the ultimate alpine shell. Its storm-proof hood is even compatible with helmets. Arc’teryx Many will never need a jacket with this level of protection, but that’s the point. If it can handle the harshest mountain conditions, it’ll effortlessly handle sideways rainstorms, a ski day in a blizzard or a decade of hard use without even blinking. title: Patagonia’s Featherweight Alpine Shell Hides Next-Gen Waterproofing, and Now It’s Half Price

content: This lightweight, water-resistant anorak strips a climbing shell down to the essentials, weighs under 11 ounces and is now 50% off. Patagonia If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more Most waterproof jackets try to do too much. Patagonia set out to change that with its M10 Anorak. This jacket was created around the idea, “the more you know, the less you need.” And that’s exactly what you get with this jacket: a stripped-down alpine shell for those who would rather carry less. What’s left is a waterproof pullover that weighs a mere 10.58 ounces. This kind of next-gen tech generally features a stiff price, but thanks to this current half-off discount, the Patagonia M10 Anorak is a worthy buy. The Patagonia M10 Anorak in its winter-ready “Sizzle Red” colorway is an excellent late-season buy with this steep discount. Patagonia However, the only colorway currently on sale is the “Sizzle Red.” The “Forge Grey” product imagery is shown throughout. Waterproofing that breathes better than most And next-gen it is as the three-layer H2No performance shell uses a nanoporous membrane for premium protection. Its film is riddled with pores that are still small enough to stop raindrops but large enough to allow sweat vapor to escape. And, as the brand loves to do, it’s made without intentionally added PFAs (which is a good thing). The M10 is as stripped down as you’ll find on an alpine shell that still has all the rough-weather protection you need. Patagonia While the brand calls it a slim fit, you can easily move and layer it, both above and below this shell. Patagonia The outer layer still holds its own, as well. The lightweight 20-denier ripstop is durably light and made from 100% recycled nylon. The finish uses a water-repellent coating while the smooth jersey backing avoids that clammy feeling if you sweat a bit. Features that earn a place The M10 pulls on like a typical anorak but uses a two-way zipper that runs down the chest so you can open it up like a quarter-zip sweater. Plus the waterproof zipper tucks into a “garage” at the chin to avoid irritating rubbing. It features a climbing helmet-compatible hood with an adjustable pull that provides practical weather protection. While Patagonia lists the fit as slim, the cut is still wide enough through the shoulders for overhead movements and it tapers nicely through the torso so it sits cleanly under a harness. The hood is designed to provide maximal protection, even though it’s made to work with climbing helmets. Patagonia Sadly, there’s just one pocket. A waterproof chest pocket that doubles as a stuff sack, which means it is large enough to allow the entire jacket to pack inside itself. The vertical zippered chest pocket is the only one you’ll find on this model. Patagonia While it’s the only pocket, it’s large enough to double as a stuff sack, carrying the entire jacket inside itself. Patagonia If you are a climber, it has a loop to clip it to your harness and comes with RECCO reflector to help locate you in emergency situations. The M10 is a modern game changer, balancing a lightweight shell that has genuine storm protection. While it may have been built to handle the rigors of alpine climbing, that means it’ll handle hiking, travel and wet commutes like they’re nothing. With this over $200 discount, it’s one of the best values on a technical shell this season. title: Danner’s New Japanese Boot Reimagines an American Hiking Icon
summary: The Danner Field Legacy channels the brand’s first-ever boot made with Gore-Tex, in a version Danner Japan built for easier accessibility.
content: The Danner Field Legacy channels the brand’s first-ever boot made with Gore-Tex, in a version Danner Japan built for easier accessibility. Danner If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more Danner changed the outdoor footwear industry for good in 1979 when the Portland, Oregon-based brand decided to introduce Gore-Tex waterproof liners to footwear . Its Danner Light became the first to use this membrane with its rugged leather and nylon panels, thus creating a boot with all-weather protection. It became a genuine legend. Surprisingly, this model has found a second life in Japan, as it became a staple of Americana-obsessed streetwear. Now Danner’s Japanese arm has created a new boot built on that pioneering foundation. Danner Japan calls it the Danner Field Legacy, and it’s a new masterpiece that still keeps its inaugural DNA. The Danner Field Legacy Boots are the newest chip off the old block, reworking the legendary Light model, but with more comfort. Danner The Danner Light look, reimagined From a distance, the resemblance is uncanny. These boots come in traditional khaki and black colorways, arguably the most iconic of the original offerings. This pair also keeps the same lace hooks which gave them the classic hiking profile. Obviously, Gore-Tex is in play here as well, while the soles carry the dependable Vibram grip down below. Stitchdown construction is used as well, just like the original Light models, which means resoleing them can happen once tread wears down. The boots utilize Vibram soles for that must-have grip that works well on the trails or in the city. Danner The more modern take One of the most noticeable upgrades comes down to their improved comfort. Danner Japan utilized OrthoLite insoles for a well-improved inner cushioning. And, per Danner Japan (in translation), they ‘optimized the production process’ to make the boot ‘more within reach’ than the original (Its price shows that). The biggest upgrade on the new Field Legacy is the use of OrthoLite insoles for a much comfier ride. Danner Danner also went all out in announcing its release, tapping Takashi Kumagai, the Japanese stylist, photographer and creative director of the brand GDC, who has worn the Light boots since high school. In the video, the Field Legacy are stated as rugged boots with the presence of sneaker-like lightness — a combo you can wear on the trails or around town. The Danner Field Legacy Boots build on one of the most influential boots in outdoor history. This version just adds on comfort and a more approachable price. This pair keeps the iconic leather, nylon canvas and Gore-Tex design in a timeless hiking boot aesthetic. Danner Availability and pricing The Danner Field Legacy Boots are now available in “Khaki” and “Black” colorways in men’s U.S. sizes 6.5 to 10. They can be bought through Stumptown Boots & Recrafting’s online store for ¥35,200 (about $223). title: Kith’s Sith-Coded Retro Sneaker Pays Homage to Its Empire State Roots
summary: This marks a full-circle moment for Fieg, as it sees the revival of a shoe he worked on years before Kith was founded.
content: This marks a full-circle moment for Ronnie Fieg, as it sees the revival of a shoe he worked on years before Kith was founded. Kith If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more In his teenage years, long before he founded Kith , Ronnie Fieg worked for a New York footwear retailer called David Z. There, he worked his way up from stock boy to buyer. He even helped design some collaborative shoes. Among them was the Asics Gel-Lyte III “Black Patent,” which garnered a reasonable comparison to a certain iconic Sith Lord. Now, helming his own brand, Fieg has come full circle, launching the Kith x Asics Gel-Lyte III Remastered “Darth Vader.” Siri, play “The Imperial March.” Kith Rise, Lord Vader This fitting tribute draws heavily from the original sneaker, although there are some key differences. These sneakers pay homage to a shoe Ronnie Feig designed back in 2008. Kith For starters, like its predecessor, this shoe has premium leather overlays atop nubuck leather underlays, providing a high-quality all-around upper that boasts textural contrast, both visually and to the touch (the leather is shiny and smooth while the nubuck is fuzzy and soft). The upper boasts contrasting materials: black, shiny premium leather and gray nubuck. Kith The Tiger Stripes on the lateral and medial sides are also made from the same premium leather as the overlays, albeit in a dark gray colorway, instead of black. The red accents extend to the tri-colored laces. Kith There are also red accents on the eyelets and trim, completing that signature sinister colorway first made famous in 1977 by the imposing villain for whom the shoe is named. I’m not sure Lord Vader would approve of you putting your toes in his face. Kith And that’s all finished off with co-branded Fieg and Asics detailing on the heels, mirrored on the inner heel. The final touch is a Darth Vader-illustrated footbed; yes, that means this is an official collaboration, unlike the original, which was simply referential. These sneakers are likely to sell out quickly, so I’d sign up for notifications if I were you. Kith The whole thing comes in specialty packaging made to resemble in-universe Imperial storage containers, adding to the overall Dark Side vibe. This official collaboration wouldn’t be complete without a specialty Star Wars-inspired case. Kith Pricing and availability Unfortunately, pricing has not yet been unveiled. That said the Kith x Asics Gel-Lyte III Remastered “Darth Vader” will launch at Kith London on Friday, November 20th, followed by the global release on Wednesday, November 25th, in-store, online, and on the Kith App at 11 AM. Drawings are open on the Kith App now, and early access will be granted to select Loyalty Members. You can also sign up for stock notifications directly through Kith’s site. content: Dating back to archival styles from the 1940s, Red Wing’s Plain Toe boot returns home for the first time in a decade. Red Wing Shoes If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more The Red Wing Round Toe has it all: good looks, a rugged build and a deep history that dates back to 1941. That’s when Red Wing first released Style No. 777, which later evolved into the Round Toe that fans know and love today. Just one problem. For the last decade, the Round Toe has belonged to a unique class of Japan- and Europe-exclusive Red Wing boots that, despite being made in America, can only be found overseas. The Round Toe boot is back in the US for good, thanks to the reintroduction of Style No. 9111. Red Wing Shoes That just changed, thanks to the reintroduction of Style No. 9111, a handsome round-toe boot fashioned out of Red Wing’s Copper Rough & Tough leather. Style No. 9111 features patina-loving Copper Rough & Tough leather. Red Wing Shoes A seamless fit Like the ever-iconic Classic Moc, the Round Toe sits atop a Traction Tred outsole, fixed to that patina-loving upper via a Goodyear Welt. And while the simple toe may be its namesake feature, it’s not the true defining trait. The Round Toe features something Red Wing dubs a “seamless back” construction first introduced on the Style No. 777. Despite the name, the Round Toe boot’s signature feature can be found on the heel: a “seamless back” constructed out of a single piece of leather. Red Wing Shoes According to Red Wing, the result is a boot that conforms more naturally to the foot while reducing friction and failure points, including those that could allow water to seep in. For the record, Style No. 9111 is actually the third Plain Toe boot to make it to US shoppers this month. However, it may be the only one that sticks around. The boot features a Traction Tred outsole, fixed to the upper via a Goodyear Welt. Neither included Copper Rough & Tough leather made by Red Wing’s own subsidiary, S.B. Foot Tanning Company. title: Salomon’s Iconic Waterproof Town-to-Trail Sneaker Just Got an Outdoorsy Makeover

content: Despite its original intent over a decade ago, the XT-6 has never looked more like a trail shoe before. Salomon If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more Over a decade ago, Salomon tapped its S/Lab division to help create what would become a foundational sneaker in the gorpcore movement. And while that shoe, the XT-6 , continually becomes distanced from its trail-ready origins, the latest take on the silhouette gets back to its roots with a new outdoorsy aesthetic. Salomon’s iconic XT-6 was originally designed for trail running but has become a foundational gorpcore sneaker over the past decade. Now, it’s all-brown upper reminds us of its original intent. Salomon The XT-6 Back in 2013, after gathering input from professional and elite trail runners and mountain sports athletes, Salomon assembled an ultra-marathon shoe that could handle the grueling demands of technical terrain over hundreds of miles. The XT-6 didn’t reinvent the wheel but balanced lightweight construction with stability and protection underfoot. It featured a streamlined silhouette that also visibly showcased its layered construction and aggressive tech. For the task, Salomon employs the waterproof Gore-Tex version of the sneaker. Salomon As the years went on, the XT-6 gradually transcended its trail-running origins, finding an entirely new audience among fashionistas, sneaker enthusiasts and eventually the broader streetwear community. However, a few years ago, the French footwear brand dropped a Gore-Tex-lined version of the sneaker, furthering its capability when facing the elements. While the XT-6 doesn’t make its way back to the trail as often as before, the newest variant serves as a nice reminder of its original intent. Brown covers the closed mesh uppers with various takes on the hue throughout the silhouette. Salomon Trail vibes The latest take on the XT-6 lands with a mostly brown upper. Construction remains the same as usual, featuring closed mesh on the upper with “anti-debris properties” and backed by a waterproof Gore-Tex ePE membrane. For the synthetic mudguard, the brown shifts to a more auburn hue as it transitions to the base. Underfoot, the midsole is embedded with a translucent teal Agile Chassis System (ACS) to support the foot. Black is used for the tongue. This variant sports Salomon’s beloved QuickLace system for fine-tuning your fit on the go. Salomon Like most Salomon sneakers, these also get the beloved QuickLace system with SensiFit for a super snug fit. Meanwhile, a Mud ContaGrip rubber outsole offers great traction on various terrain. title: Shower Thoughts: What the Heck Is With American Shoe Sizes?
summary: A medieval measurement system still governs every pair of shoes sold in America — and the math behind your size is stranger than you'd expect.
content: Gear Patrol Studios A medieval measurement system still governs every pair of shoes sold in America — and the math behind your size is stranger than you’d expect. Welcome to Shower Thoughts of a Gear Head, where we chase down the surprisingly complicated answers to questions that show up uninvited at 7 a.m , in partnership with Klarna . Because when you’re not worried about money you’re free to think about anything else. Your shoe size is built on a grain of barley. Not metaphorically — literally. The number stamped inside every pair of sneakers, boots and dress shoes you own traces back to a 1324 royal decree by King Edward II of England, who established that three dried barleycorns laid end-to-end equaled one inch. That single medieval measurement became the foundational unit of British and American shoe sizing, and no one has ever really replaced it. The barleycorn: a 700-year-old unit that became the foundation of American sizing The barleycorn measures one-third of an inch. Under Edward II’s system, that became the standard increment between whole shoe sizes — with half sizes later established at one-sixth of an inch. On the Brannock Device, sizes begin at 7⅔ inches of foot length, and each additional barleycorn adds one size. A men’s size 10 corresponds to 10⅔ inches. That math is 700 years old and still running in the background every time you ask for your size at a shoe store. How the system was codified — and where it broke down globally (US vs. UK vs. EU) The US and UK both inherited the barleycorn increment, but American manufacturers shifted the zero-point in the 19th century, leaving US and UK sizes roughly one full size apart despite using identical math. In 1880, New York businessman Edwin B. Simpson added another layer: a proportional width system built on the alphabetical scale — AAA through EEE — that American sizing still uses today. Continental Europe went a different direction entirely, adopting the Paris point (two-thirds of a centimeter) as its size increment, which is why EU sizes land in the low 40s when yours is a 10. Meanwhile, Japan seems to be the only country that used their heads to measure their feet: Japanese sizing uses centimeters directly, so a Japanese size 27 is a 27-centimeter foot. Same planet, four different answers. The Brannock Device and why even the ‘fix’ didn’t fully fix it In 1925, a 22-year-old named Charles F. Brannock built a measuring tool in Syracuse, New York, that could simultaneously read heel-to-toe length, arch length and foot width. US Patent #1,636,089 followed in 1927. The Brannock Device standardized the measurement process — but it couldn’t standardize the shoes themselves. Every brand builds its footwear on a last, an internal mold that determines the shape and fit of a finished shoe. Lasts vary by brand, by silhouette and sometimes by season, which is why a runner from one label might fit as an 11.5 while a casual sneaker from another fits as an 11 and a boot fits as a 10.5. The Brannock tells you the dimensions of your foot; it cannot tell you how the shoe was built. What sizing variation means for buyers today — and how to actually find your size The practical takeaway: your “size” is a starting point, not a guarantee. The US men’s formula — multiply foot length in inches by three, then subtract 22 — gives you a number to anchor on. (Women’s: multiply by three, subtract 21.) From there, the last wins. Reading brand-specific size guides, checking fit notes in reviews and understanding that width matters as much as length are the actual tools. If you have access to a Brannock Device, use it and note both the heel-to-toe and the arch measurement — the arch number sometimes points to a better fit than the overall length does.

title: Harley-Davidson’s Most Classically Styled Moto Is Secretly One of Its Best
summary: Test-riding the aptly named Heritage Classic goes to show its performance chops are just as on point as its throwback looks.
content: Test-riding the aptly named Heritage Classic goes to show its performance chops are just as on point as its throwback looks. Photo by Steve Mazzucchi for Gear Patrol If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more This week brought big news from Harley-Davidson, as the brand announced a bunch of 2027 models, highlighted by the new Road King ST, joined by its high-performance siblings, the Street Glide ST and Road Glide ST . Another headline is the Super Glide and Deadwood becoming part of the regular cruiser lineup, now eight bikes strong. The Heritage Classic returns for 2027 largely unchanged from its predecessor (shown), a deliberate decision that keeps a near-perfect formula intact. Photo by Steve Mazzucchi for Gear Patrol Amid all the hype, I was equally stoked to see the Heritage Classic returning for 2027, as I recently got a chance to put in well over 500 miles on its predecessor between New York City and Virginia. The new edition is not hugely different from the 2026 model, beyond new colorways of course, which is a damn good thing. The Heritage Classic’s windshield is fully detachable, letting riders switch between touring and open-air configurations. Photo by Steve Mazzucchi for Gear Patrol Because while it’s not necessarily for everyone, this bike’s unique blend of retro styling, heart-pumping power, easy ridability and quiet modern convenience is already just about perfect. Here are a few quick takeaways after several hours in the saddle. 1. Style This note pretty much speaks for itself, but tip to tail the throwback aesthetics are about as on-point as can be. The bevy of retro styling cues drape a motorcycle with such a classic silhouette, nothing looks out of place. Photo by Steve Mazzucchi for Gear Patrol Highlights include the big round trio of LED headlights, round (mostly) analog instrument panel, contoured front fender, bubbly (detachable) windshield, teardrop tank and low-slung seat, plus premium paint and glittering chrome accents. In a nod to bikes of early eras, the contoured front fender covers very nearly half of the tire. Photo by Steve Mazzucchi for Gear Patrol The overall effect is a veritable time machine, as when I rolled from the open road to an ancient diner in Pennsylvania and ordered a root beer, chicken sandwich and chocolate chip cookies, it might as well have been 1956. 2. Performance Of course, a real 1956 rider would have likely been gobsmacked by what the bike’s Milwaukee-Eight 117 Classic engine (unchanged in the 2027 edition) brings to the table. V-twin for the win: the Heritage Classic runs Harley’s Milwaukee-Eight 117 Classic engine, displacing 117 cubic inches — more than 1,900cc. At a fitting 117 cubic inches (over 1900cc for you metric folks), the gorgeous V-twin makes 98 horsepower and 120 lb-ft of torque, smoothly delivered at a twist of the throttle and pushed through a performance-tuned 2-into-1 exhaust to emit that unmistakable Harley rumble. Shout out to the true gents and ladies of New Jersey’s Bergen County Harley-Davidson dealership, who facilitated my stint with this charming cruiser. As much as I salute smaller-displacement bikes, including Harley’s new Sprint 440 , there is nothing like motoring down the highway on a big ol’ cruiser, untroubled by even the biggest trucks as the wind rushes past and the smile spreads ever wider across your face. 3. Ridability Big as the bike is, with a wet weight of 719 pounds (same as in the 2027 edition), I dare say it is pretty approachable for anyone with a modicum of experience. The 26.3-inch seat height is a key reason a 719-pound cruiser can feel approachable to riders with moderate experience. Photo by Steve Mazzucchi for Gear Patrol On the surface, that owes largely to the seat height of 26.3 inches, which will enable the vast majority of riders to place both feet firmly on the ground; together with the bike’s low center of gravity, that makes it relatively easy to maneuver the bike at low speeds (including through some punishing NYC gridlock, for example) and park. Another significant factor is the position of the foot controls, which sit in a sweet spot between right underfoot and stretched way out in front, making the gear shift lever and rear brake easily accessible, while streamlined floorboards give you a nice place to rest your feet during long highway stretches. Slim but ample floorboards let you rest your feet as you roll down the highway. Photo by Steve Mazzucchi for Gear Patrol Behind the scenes, of course, the bike boasts loads of rider-safety enhancements: ABS, TCS (traction control) and DSCS (drag-torque slip control) as well as cornering-enhanced ABS, TCS and DSCS. During most riding, these features feel virtually invisible until they kick and potentially save your life — or at least prevent you from skidding out. Meanwhile, the three easily switchable ride modes (Road, Sport and Rain) come in handy in variable conditions (including a persistent drizzle during part of the journey) and cruise control is a blessing on long stretches of highway. 4. Convenience When it comes to long-distance riding, I’ve come to realize that a bit of built-in luggage capacity goes a long way. Classically styled locking saddlebags provide enough storage for a long weekend trip. Photo by Steve Mazzucchi for Gear Patrol While the Heritage Classic does not offer the storage space present in Harley’s long-haul-focused (and significantly pricier) Grand American Touring bikes, the 1.6 cubic feet of room in the locking symmetrical saddlebags is plenty for an extended weekend trip, enabling you to ride free (as I did), with nary a backpack or tank bag weighing you down. That sort of convenience left me feeling a lot more comfortable than another Harley rider I encountered at a traffic light on the very last mile of my trip. Clad in a half helmet, clear glasses and classic biker gear, he admittedly looked pretty cool on his low-riding chopper complete with ape-hanger bars. A performance-tuned 2-into-1 exhaust channels the engine’s output and produces the Heritage Classic’s unmistakable Harley rumble. Photo by Steve Mazzucchi for Gear Patrol But when he looked me up and down and gave a nod of approval just before the light turned green and we raced into the night, hey, I felt pretty cool too. Availability and pricing The 2026 Harley-Davidson Heritage Classic is available now starting at $19,999. The 2027 edition has begun rolling into dealerships starting at $20,149. title: G-Shock’s New CasiOak Borrows Another Feature from Its Luxury Doppelganger
summary: This one feature brings it closer to the Royal Oak than ever before. It's now available in the US.
content: This one feature brings it closer to the Royal Oak than ever before. It’s now available in the US. G-Shock If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more Shortly after its debut in 2019, G-Shock’s 2100 started getting comparisons to Audemars Piguet’s iconic Royal Oak . The 2100 oozed with sports watch vibes and featured an octagonal bezel just like the AP watch. Fans were quick to dub it the “CasiOak,” and the name stuck. (In a deep-dive story, Hodinkee credits watch enthusiast Steven Davila in the Scottish Watches Facebook Group with coining the phrase.) G-Shock’s 2100 series earned the name “CasiOak” for its resemblance to the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak. Now with a new dial pattern, that comp is more true than ever. G-Shock However, the 2100 has amassed such a following over the past seven years that it’s transcended those early comps to become a streetwear staple in its own right. Hundreds of variants and colorways have dropped in the meantime, but this latest iteration borrows a subtle element from its luxury Swiss doppelganger. The Royal Oak has been known for its Tapisserie dial pattern since its launch in 1972. G-Shock Creating an icon Debuting alongside the watch in 1972, the Royal Oak’s Tapisserie dial is one of the most recognizable designs in modern watchmaking. In the early ‘70s, AP’s dialmaker Stern Frères used seven vintage guilloché-copying machines to create 300 potential patterns for the upcoming Royal Oak. The team eventually narrowed the selection to 13 designs for prototypes, ultimately settling on T21, or Tapisserie 21, which became the original Petite Tapisserie pattern. Far more intricate than a printed checkerboard, the design is mechanically engraved into a brass dial blank using a pantograph-style guilloché machine and a precision cutting tool known as a burin. The result is a series of hundreds of raised pyramids with square bases, separated by diamond-shaped recesses. Perhaps the most commonly used color on the Tapisserie pattern is AP’s signature “ Bleu Nuit, Nuage 50 ,” basically a highly specific steel blue hue. But plenty of other colors have been featured as well. Part of the Luxe Black collection, the new 2100 features a raised checker pattern across the dial and some other refined details like the blue bezel ring and all-black aesthetic. G-Shock Tapisserie twin For its newest CasiOak, G-Shock doesn’t employ any vintage guilloché-copying machines but it does evoke the very Tapisserie pattern used for the Royal Oak. The debut reference in this variant, GBM-2100LXB-1A2, is the latest entry in the Luxe Black collection. These are effectively dressed-up takes on the 2100, with previous variants sporting stealthy aesthetics and a reworked dial with a subtle grated pattern. But it was nowhere near what we’re seeing today. This is still the same 2100 under the hood, with a Tough Solar movement, ana-digi display and 200m of water resistance. G-Shock The new Luxe Black goes full-AP with its checker-texture dial. It’s matched with a similar pattern on the resin strap. There’s even a nod to Bleu Nuit, Nuage 50 with the specific shade used for the mode indicator hand. A different shade of blue is used on the bezel ring, surrounding the dial with a touch of color. Aside from the gray hands and indices, the watch is mostly all black, from the case to the bezel, and even the checkered dial. However, the new pattern certainly, if not slyly, brings this closer to the Royal Oak than ever before. A textured resin strap matches the checkered dial pattern. title: Panerai’s New Travel-Ready Tool Watch Combines the Brand’s Most Advanced Features

content: Now this is a vacation watch. Panerai If you buy from a link, we may earn a commission. Learn more Panerai’s long-running sponsorship of the Luna Rossa America’s Cup sailing team has produced a lot of cool watches, but none like this. Meet the new Luminor Luna Rossa GMT Experience (PAM01464), the first open-worked Luna Rosa watch and one of the most advanced Panerai watches yet. The new model combines several of the brand’s newest technological innovations, creating a seriously capable tool watch that’s ideal for travel and water sports, making it a fitting companion for the America’s Cup. Panerai’s Luna Rossa partnership enters an impressive new era with this latest watch. Panerai For starters, the 44mm case is made of Carbotech, Panerai’s proprietary carbon fiber composite . The material is produced by layering carbon fiber with a high-performance polymer called Polyether Ether Ketone. The case contains over 200 layers, making the watch incredibly durable despite its low weight. Water resistance is 100m, which is low for a Panerai but still more than you’ll likely ever need. Moving on to the movement, the watch uses the in-house Calibre P.4001/S, which is arguably the best GMT movement in the industry, at least in terms of real-world usability. For starters, the local hour hand is independently adjustable, which allows you to adjust to a new time zone without stopping the movement. Next, the GMT hand is set to rotate every 12 hours instead of 24 hours. This makes for more natural reading of your second time zone since it’s on a 12-hour scale, and a lumed AM-PM indicator at 9:00 makes it easy to distinguish between daytime and nighttime. The watch boasts a GMT complication that’s loaded with travel-friendly features. Panerai When you do have to stop the watch to synchronize your time, the movement even makes this easier, with a dedicated system that not only stops the seconds hand but immediately resets it to zero once you pull the crown out to the second position. The automatic movement is wound via an offset micro-rotor and has two mainspring barrels, with a total power reserve of a weekend-proof 72 hours. There’s a power reserve indicator on the caseback represented by a very cool lumed sapphire disc. The free-sprung balance also sits on an adjustable balance bridge for greater shock protection. The “S” in the calibre name designates this as a skeletonized movement, and it’s a very cool-looking one. The movement sports a black finish, with its mainplate featuring a naval underwater net-inspired grid design that matches the futuristic features of the watch. There’s plenty to look at on the caseback, including a power reserve indicator and micro-rotor. Panerai Then there’s the date window, which is arguably the most technically advanced feature. It’s a polarized date window that only displays the current date. The rest of the dates on the transparent silica glass date disc are completely invisible, meaning they don’t obstruct your view through the skeletonized movement. Each day when a new date appears, it’s almost like a magic trick. Availability and pricing With its lightweight sportiness and killer travel complications, Panerai may have made the ultimate vacation watch. And this is especially true when you consider the fact that this watch actually includes a literal vacation. As one of Panerai’s Experience watches, the PAM01464 allows its owners to take a trip with the brand to Naples, Italy, next spring for a Luna Rossa Experience during the America’s Cup. There, attendees will have the opportunity to go behind-the-scenes and on the water with the Italian sailing team while also exploring Panerai’s connections with its original home country. The watch is limited to just 30 examples, so the trip won’t be very crowded, and its price is only available upon request. In other words, it’s very expensive. title: Shower Thoughts: Why Do Dive Watch Bezels Only Rotate One Way?
summary: The unidirectional ratchet on every ISO-certified dive watch isn't a quirk — it's a failsafe engineered so a careless bump always errs toward getting you out of the water alive.
content: Gear Patrol Studios The unidirectional ratchet on every ISO-certified dive watch isn’t a quirk — it’s a failsafe engineered so a careless bump always errs toward getting you out of the water alive. Welcome to Shower Thoughts of a Gear Head, where we chase down the surprisingly complicated answers to questions that show up uninvited at 7 a.m, in partnership with Klarna. Because when you’re not worried about money you’re free to think about anything else. Your dive watch bezel spins only one way, and no, it is not just there to give you something to fidget with during meetings. That unidirectional ratchet is one of the simplest pieces of safety engineering in everyday carry, and it has kept divers alive since the 1950s. The life-or-death reason Before a diver enters the water, they rotate the bezel until the triangle marker lines up with the minute hand — a mechanical bookmark for elapsed bottom time. Now imagine the bezel gets bumped underwater. If it spins clockwise, the marker shifts to show less time has passed than actually has. The diver thinks they have more air remaining, stays down longer, and risks gas depletion or decompression sickness — the bends, caused by body tissues absorbing inert nitrogen under pressure during an overly long dive. A counterclockwise-only bezel removes that risk. An accidental bump makes elapsed time appear longer , prompting the diver to surface early. Early is inconvenient. Late can be fatal. Where the convention came from The unidirectional locking bezel first appeared in 1953 on the Blancpain Fifty Fathoms , developed by CEO Jean-Jacques Fiechter with French combat swimmers known as the Nageurs de Combat. Blancpain held an active patent on the mechanism, which put Rolex in an awkward spot when it launched the Submariner in 1954: early models used friction-fit bidirectional bezels precisely because Blancpain’s patent was still in force. The ISO 6425 rule ISO 6425 , first established in 1996 and updated in 2018, sets the minimum requirements for any watch marketed as a diver’s watch. A unidirectional rotating bezel protected against inadvertent rotation is on that list, alongside 100-metre water resistance, luminous legibility at 25 cm in total darkness, magnetic resistance and thermal shock testing. The safety feature became a certified standard — and the standard became a design icon. The click you feel That satisfying click is an asymmetric sawtooth detent, either 60 or 120 of them, machined into the underside of the bezel ring. Each tooth has a gradual sloped ramp on one side and a steep vertical wall on the other. Rotate counterclockwise and the spring-loaded pawl rides the ramp and snaps over each tooth; try clockwise and it hits the wall and stops. The count matters: 120 stops give 30-second increments of resolution, 60 stops give one-minute increments. Bezel inserts are most commonly crafted from aluminum or ceramic. Aluminum is lighter and easier to engrave — it is also why vintage Submariners develop that coveted faded patina — but it scratches easily. Ceramic holds its color far longer and is now standard on most modern sport watches. What to look for on your own watch Flip your watch over and look for the ISO 6425 designation to confirm it meets the full safety spec. The highlighted first 15 – 20 minutes on the bezel scale mark the critical no-decompression window most recreational dives stay within. Count the clicks on a full rotation to confirm whether you have 60 or 120 detents. Most divers today rely on electronic dive computers for real-time depth and tissue-loading data, but the unidirectional bezel remains a battery-free backup that needs no charging, no pairing and no software update — just a flick of the wrist before you go under.
